title: Cantor/Lawvere OQ: Which Types Admit Fixed-Point Theorems?
description: Open question oq-04 from the Lawvere fixed-point branch of Cantor's theorem: which types admit a Lawvere-style fixed-point theorem, and how does the diagonal (Lawvere) source of fixed points relate to the order-theoretic (Knaster–Tarski / Scott–Kleene) one satisfied by pointed dcpos? This formalization isolates two distinct fixed-point properties — the unrestricted FPP (every self-map has a fixed point, Lawvere's target) and the monotone FPP (every monotone self-map has a fixed point, the order/dcpo form) — and shows they are genuinely different: Bool is a complete lattice (so has the monotone FPP via Knaster–Tarski) yet lacks the unrestricted FPP, because the fixed-point-free map `not` is antitone, not monotone. The answer to oq-04 is therefore property-dependent: surjectivity (Lawvere) and order-completeness (Scott/Tarski) are incomparable routes to fixed points.

meta.author: Lawvere (1969), Knaster–Tarski, Scott–Kleene; formalization by researcher-10
meta.assumptions: None. Every result is machine-checked with 0 axioms and 0 sorries (foundational propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound only). Leverages Mathlib's OrderHom.lfp (Knaster–Tarski). This entry answers the classification question oq-04 by exhibiting the precise gap between the unrestricted and monotone fixed-point properties; it does not attempt the larger Gödel-coding or full dcpo/Scott-continuity development mentioned in sibling open questions.
originalContributions: HasFPP: the unrestricted fixed-point property (every self-map has a fixed point) — Lawvere's target
hasFPP_of_pointSurjective: Lawvere's fixed-point theorem in FPP form (point-surjective A→(A→B) ⟹ B has FPP)
not_hasFPP_bool / not_hasFPP_prop: Bool and Prop lack the unrestricted FPP (Cantor obstruction via fixed-point-free negation)
HasMonotoneFPP + hasMonotoneFPP_completeLattice: Knaster–Tarski — every complete lattice has the monotone FPP (order-theoretic counterpart of Lawvere, via OrderHom.lfp)
bool_monotoneFPP_but_not_FPP: the discriminating example — Bool has the monotone FPP but not the unrestricted FPP
not_not_monotone: `not : Bool→Bool` is antitone, the structural reason Bool escapes the order-completeness route
no_pointSurjection_to_powerProp: Cantor's theorem recovered — no point-surjection A→(A→Prop)

conclusion.summary: Two fixed-point properties must be distinguished. The *unrestricted* FPP (every self-map has a fixed point) is what Lawvere's theorem delivers from a point-surjection A→(A→B); it fails for Bool and Prop, the Cantor obstruction. The *monotone* FPP (every monotone self-map has a fixed point) is delivered by order completeness via Knaster–Tarski (Mathlib's OrderHom.lfp), and is the form a pointed dcpo satisfies through Scott–Kleene iteration. Bool witnesses that these are independent: it has the monotone FPP but not the unrestricted one, since the fixed-point-free `not` is antitone.
conclusion.significance: Gives a precise, verified answer to 'which types admit Lawvere fixed-point theorems': it depends on the class of maps. Surjectivity (Lawvere) and order-completeness (Scott/Tarski) are incomparable sufficient conditions, reconciled by monotonicity.
implications: Clarifies that the diagonal and order-theoretic fixed-point theorems are complementary, not nested.
Bool/Prop are the canonical separating examples between the two properties.
openQuestions: Formalize the full Scott–Kleene least-fixed-point theorem for ωScott-continuous endomaps of a pointed ω-CPO (Mathlib has the ωSup machinery in Order.OmegaCompletePartialOrder).
Characterize exactly the types with the unrestricted FPP (beyond subsingletons and Lawvere-surjective targets).
